Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT A. Francisco Gold Condominium II Bldg. EDSA corner Mapagmahal Street, Diliman, Quezon City DILG OPINION NO. J 35 S. SEP 2 s 2010 ELVIRA L. GOZUN-SUMADCHAT Gozun Engineering Works 21 MacArthur Highway, San Nicolas City of San Fernando Province of Pampanga Dear Ms. Gozun-Sumadchat: This has reference to your letter requesting for opinion on the following: 2010 1. 2. Whether or not the assignor of an Industrial Sand and Gravel Permit is required to secure a business license and mayor's permit; and Whether or not the mayor has the power to order the assignee of an Industrial Sand and Gravel Permit to stop quarrying despite possessing all the necessary legal permits and license and despite not having been cited for any violation by the municipal and provincial government, as well as by the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB); At the outset, may we refer you to Section 444 (b) (3) (iv) of Republic Act No. 7160,- otherwise known as the "Local Government Code of 1991", which provides the legal basis of the municipal mayor's power to issue licenses and permits, to wit: "Section 444. The Chief Executive: Powers, Duties, Functions and Compensation. - (b) For efficient, effective and economical governance the purpose of which is the general welfare of the municipality and its inhabitants pursuant to Section 161 of this Code, the municipal mayor shall: (3) Initiate and maximize the generation of resources and revenues, and apply the same to the implementation of development plans, program objectives and priorities as provided for under Section 18 of this Code, particularly those resources and revenues programmed for agro-industrial development and country-wide growth and progress, and relative thereto, shall: (iv) Issue licenses and permits and suspend or revoke the same for any violation of the conditions upon which Section 16. Genera/ Welfare. - Every local government unit shall exercise the powers expressly granted. those necessarily irnplied therefrorn, as well as powers necessary. appropriate, or incidental for its efficient and effective governance. and those which are essential to the prornotion of the general welfare. Within their respective territorial jurisdictions, local government units shall ensure and support, among other things. the preservation and enrichment of culture. promote health and safety. enhance the right of the people to a balanced ecology, encourage and support the development 01 appropriate and self-reliant scientific and technological capabilities. improve public morals. enhance economic prosperity and social justice. promote full employment among their residents, maintain peace and order, and preserve the comfort and convenience of their inhabitants.

In Roble Arrrastre, Inc. vs. Hon. Altagracia Villaflor, et. al. [G.R. No. 128509. August 22, 2006] the Supreme Court held that Section 444(b)(3)(iv) of the Local Government Code of 1991, whereby the power of the respondent mayor to issue license and permits is circumscribed, is a manifestation of the delegated police power of a municipal corporation. According to the Court, a law or an ordinance can provide the conditions upon which the power of the municipal mayor under Section 444(b)(3)(iv) can be exercised. Section 444(b)(3)(iv) of the Local Government Code of 1991 takes its cue from Section 16 thereof, which is largely an exercise of delegated police power. Clearly, the power of the municipal mayor to issue licenses and permits is founded on the general welfare clause. This delegated police power to the LGUs through its local chief executives authorizes the latter to regulate the use of property or conduct of property rights, i.e. business or practice of profession, among others, within its territory pursuant to conditions provided by law or ordinance for the common benefit of its inhabitants. In reply to your first query on whether or not the assignor or transferor of an Industrial Sand and Gravel Permit (said assignment having being duly registered with the MGB and the Office of the Governor pursuant to Section 99 of R.A. 7942, otherwise known as the "Philippine Mining Act of 1995") is required to secure a business license and mayor's permit, the answer is in the negative. Transfer or assignment of rights and obligations, particularly under the ISG permit, relieves the assignor or transferor of the obligation to secure the necessary municipal licenses and permits which springs from the operation of business or the conduct of activity within the municipality. As to your second query on whether or not the mayor has the power to order the assignee of an Industrial Sand and Gravel Permit to stop quarrying despite possessing all the necessary legal permits and license and despite not having been cited for any violation by the municipal and provincial government, as well as by the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB), the answer is also in the negative. In DILG Opinion No. 95 S. 2008, we had the occasion to discuss the limitation of the exercise of the delegated police power and the requisites for a valid exercise of police power, thus: "However, while it is beyond question that a local government unit (LGU) can exercise its police power which has been defined as the power of the State, or of the LGU, where proper, to regulate the use of property and enjoyment of life and liberty for the common good pursuant to its statutory grant under the General Welfare Clause of Section 16 of RA 7160, and pursuant to the ruling stated above, such is without limitation. To be a valid exercise of police power, two requisites must concur, to wit: there must be a lawful subject and that lawful means are undertaken in furtherance of said power. Anent the first requisite, interests of the public, in general, as distinguished from those of a particular class shall be the yardstick, before the police power is exercised. Ergo, the enjoyment of private rights may be subordinated to the interest of the greater number pursuant to the principle: the welfare of the people is the supreme law. Insofar as the second requisite is concerned "lawful means" simply refers to that time-honored principle that "the end does not justify the means". Perforce, the lawful subject must be pursued via a lawful means, failing which, shall put the police power measure at risk of being struck down as an "arbitrary intrusion of private rights"

In addition to the general requisites, the following are required in the exercise of police power by a delegate, in this case, a local government unit: (a) there must be express grant of law; (b) within territorial limits; and (c) it must not be contrary to law." While it is undisputed that property rights are subject to regulation by the State, or the LGU as in this case, there must be a valid exercise of police power. No less than the Section 1 Article Ill of the 1987 Constitution guarantees the protection of property rights through the observance of due process, to wit: "Section 1. No person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law.." In this case, absent any clear legal basis for the order of the mayor to stop quarrying, i.e. citation of the law or ordinance violated, the same may be deemed as oppressive and confiscatory hence violates the constitutional guarantee of right to due process. We hope to have enlightened you on the matter. Very truly yours, . DOQU IV . JES Director III DIR. RENATO L BRION Regional Director Brgy. Maimpis. San Fernando Pampanga MS. LOTA S.
